stories.headline: Haley Stevens' fiance hammers El-Sayed, says he'll vote for Rogers
stories.note: When a top Democrat's own fiance crosses over to Mike Rogers, the Michigan Dem rift is hard to hide.
body: Jason Turkish, the fiance of Michigan Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens, says he won't vote for Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed and will back Republican Mike Rogers instead. Turkish, a Jewish registered Democrat and Michigan lawyer, made the case Wednesday night at a Rogers event in Birmingham hosted by the Republican Jewish Coalition, according to The Detroit News.

Turkish said he had hoped El-Sayed would soften his tone after the primary but saw the opposite. "He didn't moderate, he escalated," Turkish told reporters, arguing the candidate's repeated use of the word "genocide" about Gaza makes Jewish communities less safe.

He also criticized El-Sayed's ties to streamer Hasan Piker and what he called a pattern of equivocating when asked about hateful rhetoric. Turkish, who has given to candidates in both parties, framed his vote as putting country before party.

Stevens, who narrowly lost the primary to El-Sayed, is sticking with the Democratic nominee and told CNN her household is "a house divided." Rogers, for his part, told the crowd El-Sayed has no business in the Senate if he can't recognize Iran as an enemy.

Turkish is the second person close to Stevens to break for Rogers this week, following her former campaign chair David Kramer. Stevens has not appeared publicly with El-Sayed since a unity breakfast shortly after the primary.
Why it matters: Defections from inside a top Democrat's own circle give Rogers a real opening with moderate and Jewish voters in a Michigan race that could decide Senate control.

stories.headline: Alaska's governor orders investigation after NYT report on alleged Dem-linked Senate election scheme
stories.note: An official probe into an alleged Democrat spoiler scheme puts Peltola's campaign on defense days before the vote.
body: Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy has directed the state Department of Public Safety to investigate an alleged Democrat-linked effort to confuse voters in the U.S. Senate race. The move follows a New York Times report on recruiting candidates, including one who shares nearly the same name as Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan.

The ballot lists both the incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan, and a retired teacher with no party affiliation named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. According to the Times, Democrat Mary Peltola's team worked with people trying to recruit that candidate, and the broader effort sought other would-be spoilers to dilute the senator's support.

Dunleavy said the reporting backs up what the state's Division of Elections found when it looked into the same concerns in June. He said investigators will determine whether criminal charges or civil action are warranted, adding that anyone who broke the law "must be held accountable."

Separately, the Justice Department sued on Oct. 22 to potentially delay certification if Sullivan loses by a margin the look-alike candidate's votes could have changed. Sen. Sullivan told Sean Hannity that Peltola has nothing to run on and still hasn't apologized.
Peltola's campaign told the Times it had no involvement with either Sullivan campaign and recruited no candidates. It didn't immediately respond to Fox News Digital.
Why it matters: A state criminal probe into an alleged Democrat spoiler scheme puts Peltola on defense in the final days of a key Senate race.

stories.headline: ActBlue's woes not over as top Republican predicts potential DOJ charges over foreign cash controversy
stories.note: Possible charges against the Democrats' main fundraising platform would be a major blow to the party's money machine.
body: House Administration Committee Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., says ActBlue, the Democrats' main online fundraising platform, could face criminal charges from the Justice Department. He told Fox News Digital the congressional investigation will continue regardless.

Steil said ActBlue lacked the fraud-prevention standards needed to keep foreign money out of Democratic campaigns. Whether a crime was committed is up to DOJ, he said, but if prosecutors can prove it in court, he expects them to act.

His committee, along with House Oversight and Judiciary, has spent years examining claims that loose donor verification let foreign cash into U.S. elections. Ten top ActBlue figures, including executives and founders, have pleaded the Fifth rather than answer GOP investigators' questions.

A report earlier this month found the platform's passport field only checked that a number had the right length, not that it was valid. ActBlue has since launched a passport-based identity check, which Steil said only confirms it hadn't been verifying donors abroad.
ActBlue denies wrongdoing and calls the probe a partisan attack. President Trump ordered DOJ to investigate in April 2025, but the status of that case isn't publicly known.
Why it matters: Any charges against the platform that powers most Democratic small-dollar fundraising would hit the party's money machine hard.

stories.headline: Thune goes all-in on campaign trail as Schumer stays on bench, faces rejection from fellow Dems
stories.note: Republicans' leader is out campaigning while Democrats' own candidates keep Schumer at arm's length.
body: Senate Majority Leader John Thune has been crisscrossing the country for GOP candidates, with stops in Georgia, South Carolina, Florida, Minnesota, Nebraska, Iowa and Ohio since the Senate left Washington last month. Fox News Digital caught up with him in Nebraska alongside Sen. Pete Ricketts, who faces a tight race with independent Dan Osborn.

Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, by contrast, has stuck mostly to virtual events, including a recent online fundraiser for DSA-affiliated Florida nominee Angie Nixon. Big Democratic surrogates like Barack Obama and Kamala Harris have been the ones hitting battleground states.

Several Democratic Senate hopefuls are keeping Schumer at a distance. Mississippi's Scott Colom wouldn't commit to backing him and complained that both Democratic leaders live in the same New York borough, while Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed and Kansas's Adam Hamilton have said outright they won't support him.
Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, pointed out that no Republican candidate is running against Thune as leader, while many Democrats are running against Schumer.

Thune argued Democrats' socialist wing is pulling the party out of the mainstream. "Their party has really, really drifted," he said, predicting it will cost them in what might otherwise be a decent year.
Why it matters: A united GOP behind its leader versus Democrats openly rejecting theirs is a contrast Republicans want voters to see days before the midterms.

stories.headline: Democrat House candidate hit with felony summons at campaign event
stories.note: A felony summons served mid-campaign is a self-inflicted wound for Democrats in a House race.
body: Lakesha Womack, the Democrat challenging Rep. Tim Moore, R-N.C., in North Carolina's 14th District, says she was served a felony summons when she arrived at a campaign event in Polk County on Oct. 11.

The Mecklenburg County Sheriff's Office confirmed she was served a criminal summons for felony failure to return a rented vehicle, though it didn't confirm the setting. The case stems from a 2019 rental car and records show it was opened in January 2020.

In Facebook videos, Womack said she was homeless at the time and couldn't afford the car, and that she only learned of the pending felony days before being served. She acknowledged owing money and said she thought the matter had been resolved; one of those videos appears to have since been deleted.

Moore's campaign said the episode raises serious questions, noting her court date falls a week after the election. "When the rental agreement ends, so does your right to keep the car," the campaign quipped.
If convicted, Womack could face four to 24 months behind bars or community service.
Why it matters: A pending felony case hanging over a Democratic challenger makes Moore's path to re-election in the district even easier.

stories.headline: Manhunt underway for violent illegal immigrant who was released under NYC sanctuary policies
stories.note: A fugitive freed under sanctuary rules underscores the GOP case against Democrat-run cities' immigration policies.
body: Federal authorities are searching for Alpha Bah, an illegal immigrant from Guinea who was released by New York City despite charges of assaulting a police officer with a deadly weapon, Fox News Digital reported first.

ICE lodged a detainer with Queens Central Booking on Oct. 7, but the NYPD released Bah without notifying immigration officials. It was the second time: after a June arrest for trying to get transportation without paying, the city also ignored an ICE detainer.
DHS says Bah crossed the border illegally in November 2023 and was released before ICE could request a detainer after a January 2025 trespassing arrest under Biden-era policies.
DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin blamed sanctuary politicians and called on Gov. Kathy Hochul and Mayor Zohran Mamdani to end those policies "before another American gets hurt, or worse."

Hochul signed a law in May barring New York police agencies from formal agreements with ICE, and Mamdani has reaffirmed the city's sanctuary status by executive order. Neither office immediately responded to Fox News Digital.
Why it matters: A violent suspect back on the streets after two ignored detainers gives Republicans a concrete example in their case against Democrat-run sanctuary cities.

stories.headline: Dem AG’s ‘too many golf courses’ remark goes viral as critics tee off
stories.note: A viral, out-of-touch line from a Democratic attorney general gives critics an easy target.
body: Arizona Democratic Attorney General Kris Mayes is taking heat for telling Politico the state has "way, way too much grass" and probably "too many golf courses." The comment came during a conversation about water conservation and data centers.

Her Republican opponent, state Senate President Warren Petersen, pounced, saying golf supports jobs, tourism and small businesses and that Mayes should focus on enforcing the law. He also posted that while Mayes promises to get rid of golf courses, he promises to get rid of Mayes.
Rep. Eli Crane, R-Ariz., and others piled on, and the Arizona Chamber of Commerce noted golf's roughly $6 billion economic impact and 66,000 jobs, while using 2% or less of the state's water.

Mayes said her words were taken out of context. "Relax, nobody's closing golf courses," she posted, saying she wants incentives to replace thirsty grass and wants to go after foreign mega-farms and data centers using the state's water.
Critics called her response condescending, and some voters online said the remark cost her their support.
Why it matters: Right here in Arizona, a viral misstep gives Petersen an easy, relatable attack in the final days of a close attorney general race.
